div1.head: Interview with Ray Haserodt and Mrs. Haserodt [06/19/2001]

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: this is the oral history of World War II veteran Ray L. Haserodt. Mr. Haserodt was in the U.S. Army third battalion 119th regiment, 30th infantry division. Mr. Haserodt served in the european theater and his highest rank was t-5. I am Tom Swope and we recorded this at Mr. Haserodt's home in Novelty, Ohio, on June 19th of 2001. Ray's age at the time was 77.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: okay. What was your hometown during the war?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: my home town was Lyndhurst. Lyndhurst, Ohio. That's where I was drafted from by Mrs. India Bryant. (?)Draft board. We were drafted from the terminal tower, in the train station down below, we were given a rough type of going over, very rough, and then taken and put on the train and went to Camp Perry and spent about a week in Camp Perry where everybody asked for the air corps. And, so, one day after about a week we were loaded on a train and told we were heading for a camp but nobody said where. So, the next two days the train headed south, went through Cincinnati, got onto the southern railway with their big green engines with the light drivers, steam engines at that time, ended up in Camp Shelby, and then we all realized that we were in the infantry no matter where you wanted to be.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: why do you think everybody wanted to be in the air corps?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: that was a type of a glamorous thing, I think, for a young fellow. I enjoyed airplanes and a lot of people did, so, that was the first choice, but I think at that time the invasion of Europe was being planned and the troops necessary for that were being trained, that's what we were--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: when was this exactly?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: this was in May of 1943 and--May? March of 1943. Right. And then I just spent a year in basic training at Camp Shelby in the 69th division, 271st regiment, regimental headquarters company. Studied radio, 284 radios and basically which was the type of radio used for communication between regiment and battalion and battalion--between battalions. We learned the morse code, spent more time learning the morse code which we never used in combat, but that was part of the training. We were--I took the test for the air corps after about a year after I completed basic training, and after that I was decided--the company commander decided that if I wanted to get in the air corps I should go overseas and do it, so I was transferred out of the 69th division and with a couple of my buddies were then sent overseas as replacements. I went to--by train to Camp Kilmer, new jersey, and from there to New York city and I got on the Niew Amsterdam, a big dutch boat, that was a big cruise ship, huge cruise ship. Niew Amsterdam spelled N-i-e-w Amsterdam. Dutch spelling. We went across the ocean by ourselves. The ship was fast enough apparently to outrun submarines, so we zigzagged across the Atlantic, took about probably a week, I would think, I don't exactly remember, and we ended up in Glasgow, Scotland, and we were the thing parked out in the middle of the harbor, and we were unloaded by tugs and boats because the thing--it was too big a boat to go into the docks apparently. We went by train down to Taunton, England, which is on the southwest corner of England, and then to a repot depot camp.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: what is a repo depot camp?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: replacement camp. That was the name given at the time was repo depot. There were about, I would guess, 2,000 to 3,000 fellows there, and we--this was in May of 1944. And we viewed all the airplanes and gliders and all the things were being prepared for the invasion. We watched the training of that, they could--they were flying over all the time. We heard there was going to be an invasion but nobody knew exactly when. We stayed in this camp--I stayed in this camp probably a month, a little more than a month. Did kp a couple of times.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: didn't care for that?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: didn't care for that. They had great big pans that you could crawl into that--and they had cold water to wash them with which was--oh, that was awful. Anyway, we were then told that the invasion had happened and some news was given out about it. Went through an air raid in--close to London. We were then--one day we were told that--to get packed up, we were ready to go overseas, over the channel. So, we were driven by truck to South Hampton, and loaded on an LCI, and we went across the channel without any incident, and landed on Omaha beach, Normandy, on July the 4th, and walked--I remember walking across the beach and seeing all the blown up ships and everything else that was still laying all over the place there, piles of stuff that had been brought in. We walked over to the base of the cliff and when we got over there there was a German airplane came over with--flying so low I could see the guy flying it. He was a bomber, but he didn't do anything. I guess he was just taking pictures or trying to figure out what was going on.

So, that was my first view of the German army. But we then walked up the top of the cliff on a road that was cut into the side of it, and at the top of the cliff there was a huge hole that was probably 50 feet, 70 feet in diameter and probably 20, 30 feet deep, and we asked the guy what in the world made that hole. And he said, "well, that was from the naval guns," he said. During the invasion the navy came up and fired shells into the thing and he said, "they have some big shells," and they do, they were huge. But, we then walked, marched back--walked, didn't march, probably five miles and we could hear the front, the guns at the front at the time. Walked into a field and there was a bunch of slip trenches dug and we were told to pick out a slip trench and get ready for supper, whatever k ration, whatever, so we did that, and saw some trucks going by with kind of a funny load in them, but they was two and a half tons trucks, and next morning--it got dark, then we had our k ration and got up the next morning and a truck went by again and what it was was bodies. Two and a half ton truck loads of bodies coming back from the front. It was the first experience of war, horrors of war.

And we then were marched up to the front where we met the company that was going to be with which was third battalion headquarters company, the 119th regiment, and I met a fellow by the name of Paul Ryan who was sergeant and he was in charge of the radio section, and Paul introduced me to the other fellows and said that--he said he needed a jeep driver, which carried the radios, so forth. He said, "would you want the job?" and I said, "yeah, why not?" and he said, "fine," he says--I learned later on that the fellow was killed that was driving that jeep before me, it was an air burst that had killed him. So that was my first responsibility. So, we went up to the front, I think, the next day or so, and we--I was put on guard duty and given a slip transfer, a fellow, a friend of mine, fellow's name was Burman from New Jersey, and he was on one side of the road and I was on the other and we were told there were some German patrols in the area, so to be careful.

So it was a little town in Normandy and it was kind of a dark night and there was--there was a dirt road with kind of light dirt, and there was a barn where there was a little tiny fire right up on the top where a shell had hit it, and we sat there talking back and forth, and the next thing we saw was some feet coming down the road, all you could see was the feet because--the dirt was light but everything else was black. So, they got close, and, so, we stopped and yelled out, "give the password!" So, the feet stopped. All we could see was the feet and they just stopped. Nothing happened. So, we challenged him again, we said, "give the password or we're going to start shooting!" and I released the safety on my rifle. And then it turned around, here it was a mule. I just about shot a mule. First experience. So, that was my first experience.

There was also a gas alert that night, the rear echelon, everybody started shooting their rifles off for a gas attack which was a false thing, somebody--but it scared the dickens out of you when you're on the front lines, so, anyway, the--we went in, we were the right flank of the 29th division, and our Colonel, Colonel Edney was then transferred as the next major battle that they were going to go through was the battle for saint-lo. And the 29th division was given the job of taking that and we were given the job of clearing the right flank for the 29th division, so, we lost a lot of guys doing that. We were--I got the bronze star up near that.

The battle that we were in was one where the Germans had counter-attacked from Saint-Lo, were trying to get around the back of Saint-Lo, I think, but, anyway, there were a bunch of tanks and a bunch of infantry, and we were in the middle of a field, we dug in and the jeep was hit by shells, and, so, we took the radio out and operated it by the side. And while we were there, a p-47--luckily this is in hedgerow country, but a p-47 was shot down and came diving right down at us at full tilt and hit right just on the other side of the hedgerow and all you could see was parts from that airplane was flying all over everything. So, we lost quite a few people there, but we got a lot of tanks, and, so, we did take care of the right flank of the 29th division and the 29th division under Colonel Edney did capture Saint-Lo and they had a tremendous loss of life doing it, but Colonel Edney was not respected for being--conserving about lives, he did take his objectives but he was pretty rough on people. They did take Saint-Lo.

In the meantime, the British were sitting at Caen. But, anyway, we then were told that our next objective would be a part of the front line that General Bradley had designated to be a saturation bombing and the release of the army from Normandy, and, so, our battalion, the third battalion of the 118th was the lead battalion on that, we fought up and established the line where they wanted us to be and then saturation bombing was going to be right ahead of us, so, the day be--the day it was supposed to happen, which I think was the 24th of July, the bombers came over but it was kind of a cloudy day and they dropped some bombs, but then the thing was called off, and dropped a few on us. The next day, well, we as understand it, the air corps was supposed to fly parallel with the lines so that they wouldn't fly over us and accidentally drop bombs on us, but they turned that down and insisted on coming from our rear.

And, so, the next day we fired phosphorus shells into the German lines where they wanted the bombs dropped, and so the phosphorus shells burned and that was the target for the air corps and they came over and it was an absolutely awesome site to see 2000 b-17's flying over you, the roar that--that really was an awful thing to see. Humbling, I guess, or I don't know what you would call it, but scary, actually would be scary, but they started dropping bombs and they dropped them just ahead of us. And they kept dropping them. We saw about three of them shot down, spun down in and some parachutes came up and they kept coming and coming and more bombs and more bombs, and the earth just shook, and it was terrifying actually.

I would have hated to be underneath where the Germans were over there. But anyway, after about a half hour or hour of this, the dust and--the dirt and dust and all the stuff just went up in a great big cloud and the air corps could no longer see the ground, but they kept bombing, and, so, they kept bombing into this cloud of debris and dust and so forth, and, unfortunately, the air was--wind was blowing towards us, so this whole column of dust ended up over us and then, of course, then the air corps bombed us.

And, so, we lost about half the battalion and I was--I had one land about probably a hundred feet from me which it picks you up and it drops you. Buried a guy that fortunately was just on the other side of another hedgerow, but that was--after that we--I was given the job of taking wounded back. Actually there wasn't much--the battalion was so decimated, there wasn't a heck of a lot that we could do actually, but I spent the next three hours just hauling people back, three hours or half a day, just hauling wounded back to the rear and they came back up, I finally got done, was about--just about dark and I found Ryan again, Sergeant Ryan, and then we found a fox hole and we turned in for the night there with not really having accomplished an awful lot. But, that night there was a tremendous roar over to our right. General McNair was killed close to us, also by a bomb, but there was a tremendous roar over to our right and we heard this all night long and we didn't really know what the heck was going on, but what had happened was that Patton and the third army bulldozed another road beside the one that we were on, through the hedgerows, and that's how they--the Normandy thing got out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: break out?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: break out of Normandy. It was screwed up but yet it worked. All because of the fact the Germans could not recover fast enough from that tremendous shellacking. They didn't have the people to come back and plug the hole that had been created there, which we couldn't take advantage of because we were--half of us was gone. But that was the story of the Normandy.

And then after that we were--Patton couldn't pass through us and was in the back areas of the German armies and raising all kinds of heck, I guess, but we then followed down to a town called Avranches, and from there Patton had succeeded in surrounding the lower--the other half of the German army in France there and they had about 200,000 German troops and a lot of equipment surrounded.

I learned at one of the conventions we were at later on that the British had gotten--had never captured Caen and Patton offered to go capture Caen and he was denied, he was turned down. Montgomery wouldn't allow him to do it, I guess. I don't know what the story was, but, anyway, what it did, it allowed an awful lot of the German equipment and men to get out of that pocket. There was a gap between where Patton stopped and where the British were at Caen. So, a lot of the German army got away at that point. The rest of them that were still contained in the pocket under--I forgot the General's name, but they had decided that they--the best thing, what they had to do was get out of that pocket and the best way to do it was to go towards the Brittany peninsula and, in effect, cut off Patton and cut off his oil supply, so their path was right through Avranches and Mortain.

And the 120th regiment of the 30th infantry division occupied Mortain and hill 314 was--they got up on top of this hill and in turn when this huge German attack came, they surrounded the hill, and that battalion of the 120th was isolated for, I think, a week or more, I've forgotten just how long. Anyway, it was called the lost battalion of Mortain, and we went in and relieved them, so, they had a rough time of it there. And we went in and relieved them. So, they had a rough time of it there. That was one of the major battles of our division at that time.

And after we had stopped the Germans there, we were then told that we would be chasing them, what was left--that Falaise, it was called the Falaise pocket, and that was--anyway, I forget how many--it was a major part of the German army that was captured and a whole bunch of equipment, so it was a major, major victory for the allies. Beginning of the end of the war.

But we then chased the Germans up the--up the coast, the British were on our left supposedly and we were on a path that was immediately west of Paris and we went by--we crossed--crossed the Seine river, we were--we could see Paris, but we chased, we chased the Germans. At the Seine river, we were--the Germans chose to defend that pretty heavily. We got into a field there and stopped the jeep for a minute while the lines ahead of us had stopped from a skirmish that was going on and we pulled into this thing, and got off the jeep and went over to the field and sat down on a hunk of cement there and the Germans chose to plaster that field with artillery and they did it for about two hours and they had a shell hole every six feet.

Where I was sitting, we looked down and there was a cement pit, believe it or not. The good lord had provided us the ideal foxhole. We jumped down in that thing, it was about ten of us got in there, and we survived that bombardment because of that. You know, that's one in a million you ever find a cement pit in the middle of a war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: wow

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: yeah. So, anyway, the jeep was pretty well--pretty well battered up, so I had to take it back and get it repaired and I brought it back out and met them the next day a few miles down the road. We went, we then followed the Germans and every town that we would capture they would tell us there were four tiger tanks ahead of us, and be careful. And, so, we one by one we found each tank, it was sitting in the middle of the road, had ran out of gas, and we didn't mind that one bit. That's a huge machine, oh. Took the whole road, had a hard time getting by it. Weighed, I think, 28 tons, or something like that, I've forgotten the tons. It was unbelievable. Tracks were over a foot--a yard wide.

But we then accounted for all four tanks and we captured Tournai, Belgium. The first--we were the first troops into Belgium, and while we were there we have a 28--called a 284 radio on the back of our jeep. It's an am radio, and some enterprising GI found out that if I pull out one tube in the if section, short circuited two--two connections, you could get the BBC. It changed the frequency of the set. So we got the BBC and we learned that the British had just captured--were the first troops into Belgium. So, we said, "fine, that's all right, they've been in the war a long time, they deserve it."

So we didn't think too much about it. But after we were there for a short period of time we went west then and we captured the rest of Belgium to the west and then went into Holland and my battalion was the first battalion into Holland, first American--first troops, allied troops into Holland. We captured the town of Maastricht. We were given credit for that, by the way.

So, we captured Maastricht and a lot of other towns there. We were then held up for quite awhile for supplies, and after the--or that wait was over, we eventually captured some towns in Germany, one of them being Kerkrade. This was on the German--a little over the German border, but we stayed there for quite awhile while the supplies and the rest of the thing came up, and it was then that about December they told us that we would be probably spending Christmas there, so we cut a tree and saved our boxes and so forth from home, and I think it was December 19th or so we were told to get out in the street and get ready to move, so, we did, and got into a convoy and we headed south, and went in--we drove the whole night, I remember that. Stayed at a field or someplace the next morning for awhile and then got on the road again, and we went through liege, Belgium, and didn't know where we were going.

So, we went--nobody knew where we were going actually. And, so, then we headed west from liege and we ended up in a little town called Stumont, and the battalion commander that we had had, a Courtney Brown, who had been through Italy and been an awfully good battalion commander, had been given his leave because of points. He had earned enough points, so he retired. So, we were given a new battalion commander who had never been in war before. And so, we got into Stumont in the evening, two and a half ton trucks turned around and left in a hurry. We got a small house there for our radio section, and the line companies lined up on the hill on the top around the town and nobody bothered to dig in or anything, nobody knew anything about it, and they didn't send any patrols out, they didn't do anything.

And the next morning the whole German army came over that hill, and this was the main thrust of the German army in the fall of ?Stors liege?. The first Hitler SS division, tank division, and they took us totally by surprise. We didn't even know what was going on. So, we woke up to 88's and tanks and everything else shooting through our house there, so we got orders to get the heck--get the radio and the jeep the heck out of there. So, we backed it out of there, we got it down, drove it down the road and down the road there was a--Stumont was kind of in a little pocket like, and there was a hill behind it, and then there was the road that went out of town went down an completely exposed the hill to Stumont. And at the corner where the road that we were on went to this corner, there was a big brick house and then the road turned to the left and went down this exposed hill. And I got in my jeep down to the corner and behind this house was about 200 or so GI's milling around waiting for orders to do something, and, so, we decided that we would take as many as we could on the jeep and get them at least down to the bottom of that hill.
[End of Side A]

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: So, we got 21 guys on that jeep and trailer and took off down that hill and I could see the German guys coming toward us shooting at us, and I gave it all the gas that it would take, and we had one bullet went through my legs and Ryan's legs and into the the glove compartment and another one hit me, hit the chain compartment in the back, and luckily I think we surprised the tanks, because none of them fired at us. Didn't expect us, I guess.

So, anyway, we got down to the bottom of the hill, went around that corner at the bottom going about 90 mile an hour, and stopped at the first GI's that we met and let the guys off, it was the second battalion, we were the third battalion, that was the second battalion. They were in the reserves behind us. We then went and reported to the Colonel--Lieutenant Colonel commanding the third--the second battalion and told them the situation that was going on, so then they organized a counter-attack and we went back up with them, and we recaptured--finally recaptured Stumont. In the meantime, about half of our company and half of our battalion was captured and put into a church basement in Laglace [ph], town of Laglace which is across the valley. We got back-finally got back to Stumont and then we fought back and got alongside of a big castle, I remember that. And the army pulled up a 155 long ton and--mounted on a tank, and the thing stuck 20 feet out the front of the tank and 20 feet out the back of it, and they leveled that thing and on direct-it's like firing a rifle at this town of laglace and in the town was a whole bunch of German tanks including some of the big ones, tiger tanks. One shell from that 155 long ton knocked the turret off of a tiger tank, believe it or not.

So, that was, we eventually recaptured it and recaptured our fellows. The 120th division, regiment, rather, was given the task of Malmedy, and the Malmedy, there was a bunch of them captured there, I think, for the same reason, probably were brought into battle without knowing they were in a battle, you know, and suddenly you aren't prepared. But, anyway, there was a bunch of them, had to be about 35 of them, and they were then massacred. That was the Malmedy massacre. So, that was the 120th regiment was part of our division then, and we had captured Malmedy and then we had asked for air support, and because the Germans were amassing a counter-attack on the other side of Malmedy, and, so, the air corps came over and politely bombed the heck out of Malmedy, leveled it.

And so we complained--the trouble with war in those days is you had no contact with the air corps, none whatsoever. You had to go back through corps in order to talk to the air corps. You can't talk to them. No--there's no connection, not a lot, and, so, anyway, the complaint went back through the corps, air corps apologized and came back and bombed the thing the second time. So, 120th was pretty well mauled and we relieved them.

Wasn't much left of the town, the town was pretty well leveled but there was one good thing about the whole thing. Some GI found a big pile of bricks with a cellar window, and he opened up the cellar window and down in the basement was about 40,000 bottles of white wine. Delicious white wine. Needless to say, there was a stream of GI's going in and out of that basement window until the officers caught them. Boy, that was good stuff. So, anyway, that was--after that we--the bulge was pretty near over for us anyway. We had stopped Hitler, we were given the title of Roosevelt's SS. So--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: By the Germans?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: By the Germans. Access through the valley called us through the SS.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Haserodt
sp.p: The road devils.

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Haserodt
sp.p: The red devils.

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: So, anyway, we were then sent back up, we had gone into--we had been transferred into the 9th army up in Holland and Belgium and then we were transferred back into the 1st army for the bulge, and then we were transferred back into the 9th army after the bulge was over, and we had stopped the main thrust of the German army there. But, we then went back to Kerkrade and we had--well, the first place, before that, we were in the Bulge--in the back country and the Army said they were going to give us our Christmas dinner, so they brought turkeys up and they roasted them and we ate them and, boy, they were all spoiled from--and everybody had the worst case of the GI's you ever--that was--that was a disaster.

We were in a little farmhouse, there was about 30 guys in there, and the two-holer was the only bathroom outside, and that was, that was--that was unreal, because that thing was--we called it the fertile valley when we left.

But, anyway, we then went up to Kerkrade again and we were given the job of crossing the Roer river and the Roer river at that time, the Germans had flooded it, they still controlled the dams, the headwaters which were still back in the Ardennes mountains and they flooded the Roer--they blew up the dams, so we were delayed about a week until some of the water went down, and we then crossed the Roer, attacked and crossed the Roer river, engineers built a bridge over and we were--first time I had ever seen an airplane that came over and our p-47's, there was probably 25 or 30 of them flying around overhead and this thing came over and just left them sitting still, came down, dropped a couple of bombs on us while we were trying to cross the Roer, and then when the p-47's would catch up, it would turn on its engines and left them sitting and go about 20 miles upstream or downstream rather and they would bomb--drop a couple more bombs, and then he would come back and drop a couple on us. Here it was a jet airplane, first jet aircraft I had ever seen, but the Germans had a jet aircraft bomber, twin engine.

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: I think so, I'm not sure what it was, but--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You only saw one at that time, right?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Only saw one, yeah. I've heard before, I've heard there were three of them but I only saw one at that time, yeah. I'll tell you a little more about that later on. We then were--we then, after we had successfully crossed the Roer, we were given the job of penetrating the Siegfreid line, which we did, captured I don't know how many pill boxes. Then we--after we penetrated the line, we then went south through the line, we captured the line from the side about 21 miles, and lost a whole bunch of people doing that. And then we surrounded Aachen.

The 1st division was on the bottom of Aachen and south of Aachen and we were the 30th division was the north part surrounding Aachen, so we had surrounded Aachen but the Germans had surrounded us, so we were kind of in a funny situation. We were in an air raid shelter there, and just maintaining a line around Aachen basically. Our radio was up on top and we were down inside this thing, but the Germans were shelling us pretty heavily. Our M company was just outside of the front part of the thing there. We--blew one of the guys down the mine shaft when a shell went off close to the jeep, but that was--we eventually did capture Aachen there and then we went back up north again, and were sent back for our--I think I got all this straight, but, anyway, we were sent back for training for river crossings again, and we were scheduled to cross the Rhine river with the Navy, of all people.

And, so, we went back up on the line and captured a few more towns close to the Rhine, then we went north alongside the Rhine for about 20 or 30 miles. I watched Cologne being bombed at night and it was--you could see the white flashes from the German aircraft, anti-aircraft and the orange flashes from the english bombs as they landed and it was quite a sight to see, first time I have ever seen a city bombed like that. You could sit on one side of the river and watch the whole thing on the other side of the river. It was horrifying, but it was an interesting thing to see. But the British did their bombing at night and we did our--we did it in the daytime. We then were given a section of the river and it was kept highly secret and there was another outfit that put on all 30th division uniforms, painted their jeep's with 30th division emblems and were stationed 20 miles south of us, and then we were given the job of going across the Rhine, which we did, we went across, we captured it.

And with surprisingly small amount of resistance, because apparently the decoy worked, and, so, we crossed the Rhine and captured the other side, went into Essen, captured Essen which was the headquarters of Krupp and then closed a pocket there, we captured a whole bunch of Germans. In fact, we captured so many people, we couldn't--didn't know what to do with them. I mean, they were giving up so fast that they were told just go on back, didn't even get anybody to guard them, just take off. And, so, it was quite a problem.

But we did capture the whole Essen part with the 2nd armored, I think was involved in that also. We were then put on, in conjunction with the 2nd armored and mounted tanks and 2nd armored was a good outfit and they thought a lot of us too, so, we then went across the northern part of Germany, captured Bielefeld. We went, captured a Curtvald, something-vald that was a mountain range through the middle of Germany, and the German West Point was there there, and we were successful and we lost quite a few people capturing that, that was defended pretty heavily.

We then went, I watched--before that, we captured some German officers and they wanted to know what was going on there. So, this Lieutenant organized a firing squad, and lined these three German officers up against the wall, and got the guys, their rifles, and eins, zwei, drei, and these guys never talked. They just stood at attention, so eventually he said, "drop your arms," it didn't work. But I had never seen anything like that done before. It is probably against the rules of war, I suppose.

Yeah. But, anyway, they were then called back, but we did capture that German West Point. We then went across, captured Hamm, got into Essen--not Essen. Well, it's another town where the Hermann Goering Ironworks was, and we captured a bunch of people that had been emaciated, they were in terrible shape, horrible shape, and we released them, of course, helped them. I got a flag there. Herman Goering Ironworks.

We then went a couple of towns west of there and we had to stop for awhile, I think the tanks needed retreading or something, but it was, they were getting wore out, I guess, but anyway, we stopped there and we were--some Russian people came up and said, "you've got to go see where we work." And we said, "Well, what do you mean, where where do you work? There isn't any factories around here, it's all fields." They said, "No, no, you go down and get the German fuhrer down in the village, tell us where to go." We got ahold of this fellow, and he took us up to a mine shaft with a bunch of old mine machinery, and he says, "we work down there." We said, "what do you mean you work down there?" he says, "we've got a factory down there." And they said, "well, we're going to go get the fellow to run the mine machinery and you're going to take us down there." So he did, we went and got the fellow that operated the mine machinery and we took him at gun point into the mine car and we went down with him, 1800 feet down into a salt mine and in the salt mine was a huge cavern or a passageway and off of this passageway were great big doors and you opened these doors and there would be a room that was about a hundred feet high and about 200 feet wide and about 400 feet long, unsupported ceiling, full of machinery. Full of machinery. There was a photographic laboratory, metalurgical laboratory, the whole works. And what we found out was that they built that jet airplane in that mine. The mine was about two miles long. We never did get down to the other end, but we were told that as they built this thing it was gradually put together, and when it was entirely assembled, they had a huge elevator in the middle of the town, in the town square, in fact, and they raised that whole airplane up complete onto the town square at night, hauled it off and flew it away, and that's where they built the jet airplanes, down below ground.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What town was this again?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Essen something or other. I have the name of it. Yeah, I've got the name someplace here.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Haserodt
sp.p: Isn't that incredible?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Unbelievable story, but I have one picture, the only picture I've ever seen of that place, I've never seen any other recording of that factory anywhere. There is a picture in my 30th division book of the jet aircraft down below ground.

So, we then continued to Magdeburg, and we captured Magdeburg. General Dittmar of the German army surrendered to us there. We captured the--the whole side of the Elbe river. Berlin was a hundred miles the other side of that, and we crossed the Elbe river, got into a lot of trouble and had to come back over. The Germans were coming, being chased by the Russians at such a rate that it got to be quite a scary thing, and they didn't--they all wanted to give up. We wouldn't let them. Basically, we didn't want them to. Go to the Russians.

But we had an aircraft spotter with a piper cub there and he flew over the Russian army. He said it was the darnest thing you ever saw. Said here is this column of guys going along and they've got bicycles, they've got farm wagons, they've got cars, they have anything that's got wheels on it they had and this was this column and he said in the back of it was a big wagon drawn by four horses and a big iron pot on the back of that with a fire under it. And he said they must have been making their stew going along this road. So, that was the Russian army we met there. That was where the war ended. And we--I don't recall any celebrations. We never--that was the end of it. So everybody was glad with that. We had suffered 45,000 casualties, which is 300 percent for a 15,000 unit--men unit and we were awarded 88,000 medals.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You got a bronze star specifically for what?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: For manning my radio when the jeep was blown up and we took it off the jeep and kept it going while the battle was going on, so we were awarded the bronze star for that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: purple heart?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: No, I was never wounded.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I thought you said you were hit in that jeep. It missed you, huh?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: It missed me, went between my legs.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just missed you

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Just missed us. Yeah, I don't know how it went between my legs and Ryan's and went through the glove compartment. But we then we--we then took the jeep back. After the war was over, we were put in occupation in Chemnitz, czechoslovakia.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Chemnitz, czechoslovakia or Germany?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: It's on the Czechoslovakian boarder. I don't remember. I think it's in austria actually. Well, the funny part about--another story too, when we captured those people that were emaciated, I didn't know it at the time, but starting back again, my daughter married a boy from Holland, he had migrated, him and his parents had migrated to Pelee island. We went there for vacation, my daughter met him, fell in love and married him, and we were talking later on and he had been--the father had been captured by the Germans or--and put into work detail, transferred back into Germany and my outfit released him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: So, that was a small world, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything specifically about any buddies?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: In what way? Ryan--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, any close buddies, stories about buddies or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Not basically.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Haserodt
sp.p: Captain (unintelligible).

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Well, that's part--this goes back to my training days.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Haserodt
sp.p: Training.

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: There was a fellow from New York name, was Katz and he was a little bit slow and this is on that tape, by the way, but, anyway, the captain came down the road and he was going up the company road and, he said, "hi, captain," he waived at him. The captain stopped him and said, "Look, you're supposed to salute an officer. Whenever you see them you salute and they'll salute you back." And he said, "The next time you forget we'll see if we can't do something about it." So, about a week later, here comes the captain down the road and here is Katz walking along. "hi, captain." so, captain said, "all right, Katz," so he assigned him the job, he said, "You've got to start at the top of the company road," and he says, "And you march down to the end with a full field pack and rifle, you get down to the end and you salute and you do an about face and you walk up to the other end of the company street, stop, salute, about face." So this went on for five hours, he had a five hour deal. So, when it was all over, everybody said, well, he ought to remember now, you know. And, son of a gun, about a week later here comes the captain down the road and here comes Katz, "Hi, captain."

sp.speaker: Mrs. Haserodt
sp.p: I'm sorry

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: So, they offered him a section 8, and he refused, so, you know, you can't fault him. I mean, that was just the way Katz was. Oh, golly. But our jeep, when we turned it in, had 80 holes in it, so, we were pretty well peppered. I had another experience--well, I keep thinking about things. I'm sorry I'm backtracking. Yeah, this was in--yeah, this was in northern France, before we got over the Belgium border, we were chasing some Germans and they had stopped and we were firing, so we stopped and were pulled over to the side of the road and Ryan said, "don't go all the way over," he says, "the Germans, they plant mines over there in the soft dirt," and he said, "stay away from there for cripes sake." okay. So, I stopped the thing in the middle of the road, and there were some shells flying around, but there was a beep, beep, beep, beep behind me. Ryan said, "if he wants to go around around, let him go over on the side of the road." small dirt road. And, so, beep, beep, beep, beep. And I looked around and here comes--looked up and here is General Harrison standing beside my jeep and he says, "soldier, move the jeep over so we can go by." "yes, sir." looked at Ryan. Ryan said, "move the jeep over." so, he moved the jeep over and he went by. Didn't say anything, that was the end. He was a nice guy. He was a good guy--good man. He was the guy that ended up being the negotiator at Panmunjan. Yeah. He was chief head of negotiating team at Panmunjan. General Harrison, good man.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular memories of getting letters or packages from home?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Oh, nice to get them, that was it. Yeah--no, we never got too many at any one time. We were on line for the first three months I was there, we never got off the front line much, so, there wasn't much time for that type of thing. But when we did get them, we got them in a bunch, but nothing in particular like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Does anything come to mind as your most vivid memory of that whole experience?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Oh--

sp.speaker: Mrs. Haserodt
sp.p: (inaudible.)

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Haserodt
sp.p: (inaudible.)

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Yeah, that was--we had gotten through most of the war when we had crossed the Rhine river, about a day or so and we were--had been through a shelling and we pulled over and there was a--we stopped, looked over in the field and there was a figure there with a long beard and brown coat and four sheep. And he stood there, it was probably about 500 feet from us. He didn't move and we didn't move, we didn't know what to do. And the column started up and we moved on, but you wonder about things like that in a war. It was most interesting. I think--I felt better about things after that for some reason or other, but, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Gives me chills

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. That's pretty amazing. Do you remember anything about your homecoming, any specific memories about it?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: No, I was--from Kemnitz I was given the honor of being let go first because I had the fewest points, I was a replacement, and, so, I was given the honor of getting out of there and going to Camp Lucky Strike and being sent to Japan, that was my--that was my next deal. So I was released, I got under General Black, got halfway across the Atlantic Ocean, it was a small boat. Right in the middle of the ocean the war in Japan was over, was declared over, which did not make me the least bit unhappy. So, we got--we ended up at Boston, red cross gave us some milk, first time I had milk for a long time, I remember that, and we got on the train and went to Atterbury and got a pass for home, spent about a month at home, got my wife, went back to Atterbury and was discharged. The guy asked me, "do you want to stay in the Army?" I said, "no, I think I had enough."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wanted you to reup at that point?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Yeah. So, that was my experience.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life after that?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Oh, a little bit, yeah, but I made it. Yeah, we made it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was it just because civilian life as opposed to what you were going through?

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Yeah, I don't know just what it was, but you kinda felt like you hadn't done much living and you wanted to catch up on stuff, I guess.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, that's true too.

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Yeah. But that was about the best--awful glad to be home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ray Haserodt
sp.p: Yeah.
[Conclusion of interview]
